MIXED-MOTIVE DISCHARGE UNDER FEHA AND THE EMPLOYER'S "SAME-DECISION" SHOWING (GOV. CODE § 12940(A); HARRIS V. CITY OF SANTA MONICA; ALAMO V. PRACTICE MANAGEMENT; CACI NOS. 2507, 2512) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

MIXED-MOTIVE DISCHARGE AND THE SAME-DECISION SHOWING — APPLICABILITY NOTE
This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee's former position as Bus Operator with Acme, Inc., recorded here as having ended on August 28, 2026, and Acme, Inc.'s stated reason for that decision, recorded here as: attendance and preventable accidents during probation. It describes what the California Fair Employment and Housing Act, the California Supreme Court's decision in Harris v. City of Santa Monica (2013), the Court of Appeal's decision in Alamo v. Practice Management Information Corp. (2013), and the Judicial Council's civil jury instructions say about a termination alleged to have been motivated by both a discriminatory (or retaliatory) reason and a legitimate one: the "substantial motivating factor" standard of causation, the definition of an employer's "same-decision" showing, the rule that such a showing limits remedies rather than defeating liability, which remedies are unavailable and which remain available after it, the burden and standard of proof and the pleading requirement, how juries are instructed, and how the federal Title VII rule compares. Whether any protected characteristic or activity played any part in Acme, Inc.'s decision, whether the stated reason actually motivated the decision, whether Acme, Inc. would have made the same decision at the time for that reason alone, and what relief (if any) would follow are facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties, the date, and the stated reason here does not itself establish that any of the rules described below applies to their separation, and this sheet states what the statute, the courts, and the jury instructions say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular claim or defense.

THE STATUTE AND THE QUESTION A MIXED-MOTIVE CASE PRESENTS: GOVERNMENT CODE SECTION 12940(A) AND THE LIMITS OF THE SINGLE-MOTIVE FRAMEWORK
Government Code section 12940(a) makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer, "because of" a listed protected characteristic of any person, to refuse to hire, to bar or discharge the person from employment, or to discriminate in compensation or in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment. In Harris v. City of Santa Monica (2013), the California Supreme Court explained that in FEHA cases that do not involve mixed motives it has used the three-stage McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting test, under which the plaintiff makes a prima facie case, the employer produces evidence of a legitimate reason, the plaintiff then attempts to show that reason was a pretext, and the ultimate burden of persuasion on discrimination stays with the plaintiff. The Court observed that this framework presupposes that the employer had a single reason for the adverse action that was either discriminatory or legitimate, and that in a mixed-motives case there is no single "true" reason — which raised the question of what the trier of fact is to do when it finds that a mix of discriminatory and legitimate reasons motivated the decision. The Court identified three plausible readings of the statute's causation requirement ("but for" cause, "substantial factor," and "a motivating factor") and found nothing in the FEHA's legislative history bearing on which was intended. As applied to Jordan Lee's separation from Acme, Inc., this clause identifies the statute and the interpretive question; whether any protected characteristic played any part in the decision recorded as ending on August 28, 2026 is a fact this clause does not determine.

THE PLAINTIFF'S SHOWING: DISCRIMINATION MUST BE A "SUBSTANTIAL MOTIVATING FACTOR," NOT MERELY "A MOTIVATING FACTOR"
Harris held that a FEHA plaintiff is not required to prove that discrimination was the "but for" cause of the adverse action, but must show more than that it was simply a motivating factor: the jury is to determine whether discrimination was "a substantial motivating factor/reason" for the decision. The Court explained that requiring a substantial motivating factor, rather than merely a motivating factor, more effectively ensures that liability will not be imposed on evidence of mere thoughts or passing statements unrelated to the disputed decision, and that mere discriminatory thoughts or stray remarks are not sufficient to establish liability. At the same time, the Court stated that discrimination need not be alone sufficient to bring about the decision in order to be a substantial motivating factor, and that discrimination can be serious, consequential, and even by itself determinative without also being a "but for" cause. The Court declined to say in the abstract what evidence would suffice. The Judicial Council's instruction CACI No. 2507 now defines a "substantial motivating reason" as a reason that actually contributed to the adverse action, that must be more than a remote or trivial reason, and that does not have to be the only reason motivating the action. Whether any protected characteristic was a substantial motivating reason for Acme, Inc.'s decision regarding Jordan Lee is a fact this clause does not determine.

THE EMPLOYER'S SAME-DECISION SHOWING: WHAT IT IS, AND WHY IT LIMITS REMEDIES RATHER THAN DEFEATING LIABILITY
Harris defined a "same-decision showing" as proof that the employer, in the absence of any discrimination, would have made the same decision at the time it made its actual decision. The employer had asked for an instruction under which such a showing would be a complete defense; the Court rejected that position. Relying on the FEHA's stated purposes of not only redressing but also preventing and deterring unlawful employment practices, the Court concluded that a same-decision showing is not a complete defense to liability once the plaintiff has proven that discrimination was a substantial factor motivating the adverse action, and that proof of a substantial discriminatory factor exposes the employer to liability even if other factors would have led it to make the same decision. The Court of Appeal in Alamo v. Practice Management Information Corp. (2013) summarized the result: the mixed-motive defense is available under the FEHA only as a limitation on remedies and not as a complete defense to liability, so an employer that proves it would have made the same decision is still liable, with the plaintiff's remedies limited as described in the following clauses. Whether Acme, Inc. would have terminated Jordan Lee's employment on August 28, 2026 for the stated reason (attendance and preventable accidents during probation) even absent any discriminatory motive is a fact this clause does not determine.

REMEDIES FORECLOSED BY A SAME-DECISION SHOWING: DAMAGES, BACKPAY, FRONT PAY, NONECONOMIC DAMAGES, AND REINSTATEMENT
Having held that a same-decision showing does not defeat liability, Harris turned to what relief remains. The Court rejected the plaintiff's contention that a terminated employee could still obtain reinstatement or backpay, reasoning that those remedies would not redress the adverse effects of discrimination if legitimate reasons would have led the employer to terminate the employee anyway, would award an unjustified windfall, and would unduly limit employers' freedom to make legitimate employment decisions; it said the same of any remedy for economic loss, such as front pay. On noneconomic damages the Court called the issue closer, acknowledging that a decision substantially motivated by discrimination inflicts dignitary harm, but concluded that it is unrealistic to ask a trier of fact to separate the distress caused by discrimination from the distress caused by the discharge itself, and that a termination decision substantially motivated by discrimination is not compensable in damages under section 12940(a) when the employer makes a same-decision showing. The Court's summary is that in that circumstance the plaintiff cannot be awarded damages, backpay, or an order of reinstatement. The Court added that the unavailability of noneconomic damages under the FEHA does not preclude the possibility of tort liability for intentional infliction of emotional distress. What remedies, if any, would be available to Jordan Lee is a question this clause does not resolve.

REMEDIES THAT SURVIVE A SAME-DECISION SHOWING: DECLARATORY RELIEF, INJUNCTIVE RELIEF, AND DISCRETIONARY ATTORNEY'S FEES AND COSTS
Harris held that the unavailability of damages after a same-decision showing does not make a finding of unlawful discrimination an empty gesture, and identified three consequences. First, proof that the decision was substantially motivated by discrimination may warrant a judicial declaration of employer wrongdoing (citing Code of Civil Procedure section 1060). Second, a court may grant injunctive relief where appropriate to stop discriminatory practices. Third, the plaintiff may be eligible for reasonable attorney's fees and costs under the FEHA's fee provision, which the Court explained compensates the plaintiff and counsel for bringing a meritorious claim without risking a windfall, and furthers the statute's goal of deterrence by requiring the employer to absorb the costs of litigation for which its own wrongdoing is substantially responsible. The Court stressed that a fee award is discretionary, may take into account the scale of the plaintiff's success, and must not encourage unnecessary litigation of claims that serve no public purpose. The fee provision, now Government Code section 12965(c)(6), authorizes the court in its discretion to award the prevailing party reasonable attorney's fees and costs, including expert witness fees, while limiting awards to prevailing defendants to actions that were frivolous, unreasonable, or groundless. Whether any such relief would be appropriate in Jordan Lee's case is a question this clause does not resolve.

BURDEN AND STANDARD OF PROOF, THE PLEADING REQUIREMENT, AND WHETHER THE EMPLOYER MUST CONCEDE MIXED MOTIVES
Harris allocated the burdens as follows: the plaintiff must show by a preponderance of the evidence that discrimination was a substantial factor motivating the termination; the employer is then entitled to demonstrate that legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons would have led it to make the same decision at the time; and the employer must prove that by a preponderance of the evidence, the Court rejecting the plaintiff's argument for a clear-and-convincing standard. Because the burden of the same-decision showing rests on the defendant, Harris held that it is a defense the employer should plead — that is, plead that if its actions are found to have been motivated by both discriminatory and nondiscriminatory reasons, the nondiscriminatory reasons alone would have induced it to make the same decision. In Harris itself, the City's answer, which alleged that the adverse actions were based on legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons and not on pretext, was held sufficient to put the plaintiff on notice, so the failure to plead the defense in terms did not bar a same-decision instruction. In Alamo, by contrast, the employer's answer contained no affirmative defense asserting that it had legitimate reasons for the discharge, the defense was first raised in a motion in limine about a month before trial, and the Court of Appeal held the employer had waived the defense and could not assert it on retrial. Harris also rejected the argument that an employer must concede it had mixed motives in order to make a same-decision showing, holding there is no inconsistency in arguing that its motive was legitimate while contingently arguing that, if mixed motives are found, the lawful motive alone would have led to the discharge. Whether Acme, Inc. has pleaded or could establish such a defense is a matter this clause does not determine.

Harris directed that a jury in a mixed-motive case alleging unlawful termination be instructed that it must find the employer's action was substantially motivated by discrimination before the burden shifts to the employer to make a same-decision showing, and that a same-decision showing precludes reinstatement, backpay, or damages. The Court also stated that the former BAJI No. 12.26 instruction requested by the employer — under which the employer "is not liable" if it proves its legitimate reason standing alone would have induced the same decision — was not correct insofar as it treated the showing as a complete defense. The Judicial Council responded with CACI No. 2512, given together with CACI No. 2507, which tells jurors that if discrimination or retaliation was a substantial motivating reason and the employer's stated reason was also a substantial motivating reason, they must decide whether the employer has proven it would have taken the action anyway at that time for the stated reason; that they are to determine what actually motivated the employer, not what it might have been justified in doing; and that if the employer would have taken the action anyway, the plaintiff will not be entitled to reinstatement, back pay, or damages. Its Directions for Use distinguish a mixed-motive case from a pretext case, in which the only actual motive is discriminatory and the stated reasons are fabricated. In Alamo, the Court of Appeal held it prejudicial error to have instructed a jury with the former versions of CACI Nos. 2430 (wrongful discharge in violation of public policy), 2500 (disparate treatment), 2505 (retaliation), and 2507, which required only "a motivating reason," and rejected the argument that jurors would draw no meaningful distinction between "a motivating reason" and "a substantial motivating reason." How a jury would be instructed in any proceeding involving Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. is a matter this clause does not determine.

expectedJSON.body: Harris held that the unavailability of damages after a same-decision showing does not make a finding of unlawful discrimination an empty gesture, and identified three consequences. First, proof that the decision was substantially motivated by discrimination may warrant a judicial declaration of employer wrongdoing (citing Code of Civil Procedure section 1060). Second, a court may grant injunctive relief where appropriate to stop discriminatory practices. Third, the plaintiff may be eligible for reasonable attorney's fees and costs under the FEHA's fee provision, which the Court explained compensates the plaintiff and counsel for bringing a meritorious claim without risking a windfall, and furthers the statute's goal of deterrence by requiring the employer to absorb the costs of litigation for which its own wrongdoing is substantially responsible. The Court stressed that a fee award is discretionary, may take into account the scale of the plaintiff's success, and must not encourage unnecessary litigation of claims that serve no public purpose. The fee provision, now Government Code section 12965(c)(6), authorizes the court in its discretion to award the prevailing party reasonable attorney's fees and costs, including expert witness fees, while limiting awards to prevailing defendants to actions that were frivolous, unreasonable, or groundless. Whether any such relief would be appropriate in Jordan Lee's case is a question this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Government Code § 12965 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (6) In civil actions brought under this section, the court, in its discretion, may award to the prevailing party, including the department, reasonable attorney’s fees and costs, including expert witness fees, except that, notwithstanding Section 998 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a prevailing defendant shall not be awarded fees and costs unless the court finds the action was frivolous, unreasonable, or groundless when brought, or the plaintiff continued to litigate after it clearly became so.

expectedJSON.gap: Harris cited the fee provision as section 12965, subdivision (b); the provision has since been renumbered and is quoted here from the Legislature's current text at subdivision (c)(6), which also contains the limit on fee awards to prevailing defendants (added by later legislation and not discussed in Harris). Harris's injunctive-relief point cited Aguilar v. Avis Rent A Car System, Inc. (1999) 21 Cal.4th 121 and a Seventh Circuit decision, neither of which this sheet fetches. The Court's discussion of fee discretion quoted language from earlier decisions on when fee awards are appropriate; only the Harris sentences themselves are quoted here. How a court would exercise its discretion on fees, and whether the plaintiff would be a "prevailing party" in a particular procedural posture, are questions Harris left to the trial court and this clause does not address.

expectedJSON.body: Harris allocated the burdens as follows: the plaintiff must show by a preponderance of the evidence that discrimination was a substantial factor motivating the termination; the employer is then entitled to demonstrate that legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons would have led it to make the same decision at the time; and the employer must prove that by a preponderance of the evidence, the Court rejecting the plaintiff's argument for a clear-and-convincing standard. Because the burden of the same-decision showing rests on the defendant, Harris held that it is a defense the employer should plead — that is, plead that if its actions are found to have been motivated by both discriminatory and nondiscriminatory reasons, the nondiscriminatory reasons alone would have induced it to make the same decision. In Harris itself, the City's answer, which alleged that the adverse actions were based on legitimate nondiscriminatory reasons and not on pretext, was held sufficient to put the plaintiff on notice, so the failure to plead the defense in terms did not bar a same-decision instruction. In Alamo, by contrast, the employer's answer contained no affirmative defense asserting that it had legitimate reasons for the discharge, the defense was first raised in a motion in limine about a month before trial, and the Court of Appeal held the employer had waived the defense and could not assert it on retrial. Harris also rejected the argument that an employer must concede it had mixed motives in order to make a same-decision showing, holding there is no inconsistency in arguing that its motive was legitimate while contingently arguing that, if mixed motives are found, the lawful motive alone would have led to the discharge. Whether Acme, Inc. has pleaded or could establish such a defense is a matter this clause does not determine.

If the employer proves by a preponderance of the evidence that it would have made the same decision for lawful reasons, then the plaintiff cannot be awarded damages, backpay, or an order of reinstatement.

expectedJSON.body: Harris directed that a jury in a mixed-motive case alleging unlawful termination be instructed that it must find the employer's action was substantially motivated by discrimination before the burden shifts to the employer to make a same-decision showing, and that a same-decision showing precludes reinstatement, backpay, or damages. The Court also stated that the former BAJI No. 12.26 instruction requested by the employer — under which the employer "is not liable" if it proves its legitimate reason standing alone would have induced the same decision — was not correct insofar as it treated the showing as a complete defense. The Judicial Council responded with CACI No. 2512, given together with CACI No. 2507, which tells jurors that if discrimination or retaliation was a substantial motivating reason and the employer's stated reason was also a substantial motivating reason, they must decide whether the employer has proven it would have taken the action anyway at that time for the stated reason; that they are to determine what actually motivated the employer, not what it might have been justified in doing; and that if the employer would have taken the action anyway, the plaintiff will not be entitled to reinstatement, back pay, or damages. Its Directions for Use distinguish a mixed-motive case from a pretext case, in which the only actual motive is discriminatory and the stated reasons are fabricated. In Alamo, the Court of Appeal held it prejudicial error to have instructed a jury with the former versions of CACI Nos. 2430 (wrongful discharge in violation of public policy), 2500 (disparate treatment), 2505 (retaliation), and 2507, which required only "a motivating reason," and rejected the argument that jurors would draw no meaningful distinction between "a motivating reason" and "a substantial motivating reason." How a jury would be instructed in any proceeding involving Jordan Lee and Acme, Inc. is a matter this clause does not determine.

We further conclude that the trial court’s instructional error with respect to former CACI Nos. 2430, 2500, 2505, and 2507 was prejudicial because the proper standard of causation in a FEHA discrimination or retaliation claim is not “a motivating reason,” as stated in the instructions, but rather “a substantial motivating reason,” as set forth in Harris.

expectedJSON.body: Harris drew on the federal experience under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. After the United States Supreme Court's 1989 decision in Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins, Congress amended Title VII in 1991 to provide that an unlawful employment practice is established when the complaining party demonstrates that race, color, religion, sex, or national origin was a motivating factor for any employment practice, even though other factors also motivated the practice. A companion provision states that on a claim in which an individual proves such a violation and the respondent demonstrates it would have taken the same action in the absence of the impermissible motivating factor, the court may grant declaratory relief, injunctive relief, and attorney's fees and costs directly attributable to the mixed-motive claim, but shall not award damages or order admission, reinstatement, hiring, promotion, or payment. Harris described these provisions as codifying the rule that a same-decision showing limits the remedies available to a Title VII plaintiff but does not provide a complete defense to liability, and noted they remain in effect. The California rule announced in Harris reaches a similar remedial result under the FEHA's own text and purposes, but with a "substantial motivating factor" threshold for the plaintiff's showing rather than Title VII's "a motivating factor" wording. Which statute, if any, would govern a claim by Jordan Lee is a question this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2 (Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, an unlawful employment practice is established when the complaining party demonstrates that race, color, religion, sex, or national origin was a motivating factor for any employment practice, even though other factors also motivated the practice.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5 (Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: On a claim in which an individual proves a violation under section 2000e–2(m) of this title and a respondent demonstrates that the respondent would have taken the same action in the absence of the impermissible motivating factor, the court— (i) may grant declaratory relief, injunctive relief (except as provided in clause (ii)), and attorney’s fees and costs demonstrated to be directly attributable only to the pursuit of a claim under section 2000e–2(m) of this title; and (ii) shall not award damages or issue an order requiring any admission, reinstatement, hiring, promotion, or payment, described in subparagraph (A).

citations.quote: Two years later, Congress passed the Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1991, which (among other things) codified the rule that an employer’s same-decision showing limits the remedies available to a Title VII plaintiff but does not provide a complete defense to liability.

citations.case: Harris v. City of Santa Monica (2013) 56 Cal.4th 203
citations.quote: These provisions remain in effect today.

Hopkins (1989) 490 U.S. 228, Desert Palace, Inc. v. Costa (2003) 539 U.S. 90, or Gross v. FBL Financial Services, Inc. (2009) 557 U.S. 167, all of which Harris discussed. Harris noted that Gross construed the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act as not incorporating a motivating-factor standard; Title VII's mixed-motive provisions by their terms apply only to the five listed characteristics, and the federal treatment of retaliation and of other federal statutes is outside this clause. The federal statute uses the term "complaining party" and the words "a motivating factor"; Harris's "substantial motivating factor" formulation is a construction of the FEHA, not of Title VII. Harris referred to the 1991 legislation as the "Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1991"; the enacting statute is commonly cited as the Civil Rights Act of 1991 (Pub. L. No. 102-166), a naming discrepancy this sheet reports without resolving.
